summary: Charles B. Jones is a scholar in Buddhist studies, religious studies, and sinology who earned his PhD at the University of Virginia under Paul Groner in 1996. He served as Associate Professor and Associate Dean at the Catholic University of America.
Charles Bally (1865–1947) was a linguist who studied at Humboldt University of Berlin and under Ferdinand de Saussure. He held an academic post at the University of Geneva from circa 1893 to 1939.

Charles Barbier de Meynard (1826–1908) worked in linguistics, history, archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. A student of Jules Mohl, he held posts at École des langues orientales, Collège de France (1885–1908), and the Institut de France.

Charles Burnett (born 1951) is a historian and philosopher who earned his degrees at the University of Cambridge. He held research and teaching posts at the University of Sheffield and the Warburg Institute, becoming professor there in 1999.

Charles Cutler Torrey (1863–1956) was a religious studies scholar and historian who studied under Theodor Nöldeke. He taught Semitic languages at Andover Theological Seminary (1892–1900), served as professor at Yale University (1900–1932), and founded ASOR in 1901.

Charles D. Orzech is a scholar of religious studies, Buddhist studies, and sinology who completed his doctorate at the University of Chicago. He chaired the Religious Studies Department at UNC Greensboro and was a Fellow at the National Humanities Center (2009–2010).

Charles Duroiselle (1871–1951) worked in Indology, Buddhist studies, and archaeology. He taught Pali at the University of Rangoon (~1899–1919) and served as Superintendent of the Archaeological Survey of Burma (1912–1940) and Archaeological Survey of India Burma Circle.

Charles Edmund Godakumbura (1907–1977) was an Indologist and historian. Educated at the University of London (BA, PhD, D.Litt.), he taught at SOAS and served as Commissioner of Archaeology for the Archaeological Survey of India (1956–1967).

Charles Eliot (1862–1931) was a scholar of Buddhist studies, Indology, and sinology educated at Balliol College, Oxford. He served in the Foreign Office (1886–1904), at the University of Sheffield (1905–1912), and as principal of The University of Hong Kong (1912–1918).

Charles Elliott (1776–1856) was an Indology and history scholar who worked for the East India Company and served as Treasurer of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland from circa 1836 to 1856.

Charles Gabriel Seligman (1873–1940) was a scholar of history and archaeology who studied medicine at St Thomas's Hospital. He held the chair of ethnology at the University of London and the London School of Economics from 1913 to 1934.
Charles Goodman specializes in philosophy and Buddhist studies. He earned his PhD at the University of Michigan in 2002 under Allan Gibbard and became an Associate Professor at Binghamton University.

Charles H. Long (1926–2020) was a religious studies scholar who earned his BD and PhD at the University of Chicago. He held faculty posts at Chicago, UNC Chapel Hill, Duke, Syracuse, and UC Santa Barbara.

Charles Hallisey (born 1953) is a Buddhist studies scholar who earned degrees at Colgate, Harvard, UPenn, and the University of Chicago. He taught at Loyola University Chicago, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and Harvard University.

Charles Henry Tawney (1837–1922) was an Indologist who studied and taught at Trinity College, Cambridge. He served as Principal of Presidency College, Chennai, and later as Librarian of the India Office Library (1892–1903).

Charles Malamoud (born 1929) is a scholar in Indology and religious studies who studied at the University of Paris. He taught at the University of Lyon (1962–1972) and served as Directeur d'Études at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (1979–1998).
Charles Oman (1860–1946) was a historian who studied at New College, Oxford, from circa 1878 to 1882. He subsequently held an academic post at the University of Oxford from circa 1905 to 1946.

Charles Otto Blagden (1864–1949) was a scholar in linguistics, history, and archaeology. He was educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and held an academic post at SOAS University of London from circa 1917 to 1935.

Charles Philip Brown (1798–1884) was an Indologist and linguist who studied at the East India Company College. He served in the Indian Civil Service (1817–1854) and later worked as Professor of Telugu at the University of London (1865–1879).

Charles Ramble (born 1957) is a Tibetologist and religious studies scholar who studied under Michael Aris at Durham University. He held posts at the University of Oxford and became Directeur d'études at the École Pratique des Hautes Études in 2009.
